case_studies.title: Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard
case_studies.abstract: Agent evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and inform deployment decisions, yet ranks can reflect not only the model but also the effects of the evaluation conditions such as the scaffolds or tasks. This makes reliability claim-dependent: an evaluation that reliably ranks deployed systems may not reliably rank underlying models. We ask which conclusions current agent evaluations reliably support and what additional evaluation would improve them. We develop a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework for sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards and apply it to 22 benchmarks from the H
case_studies.summary: The paper shows that rankings of AI agents can change depending on the specific tasks and conditions used in testing, meaning current leaderboards may not truly reflect an agent’s overall performance. The authors built a Bayesian model to separate out how much of the ranking variance comes from the model itself versus the evaluation setup, applied it to 22 benchmarks, and found that adding more tasks often doesn't fix ranking reliability. This is not relevant to everyday cloud infrastructure management.

It highlights that more benchmark tasks do not guarantee a more trustworthy ranking, a point that could influence how engineers interpret third‑party model comparisons. The methodology is academically interesting but lacks direct actionable steps or tools for immediate automation or risk mitigation. Consequently, the value within 90 days is modest.
